title: The Decapolis
lead: A group of Greek-style cities east and south of the Sea of Galilee, most of them east of the Jordan, with a mostly Gentile population. In the Gospels it is the Gentile land just across the lake from Jesus' home ground, where he frees the man with the legion and later heals a deaf man.

sections.b: "Decapolis" means "ten cities." Pliny the Elder lists them (Natural History 5.74): Damascus, Philadelphia (modern Amman), Raphana, Scythopolis (Beth-shean, the only one west of the Jordan), Gadara, Hippos, Dion, Pella, Gerasa (modern Jerash) and Canatha, while noting that other writers' lists differ. They had been founded or refounded as Greek cities after Alexander's conquests, were freed from Jewish rule by Pompey in 63 BC and attached to the Roman province of Syria. They had temples to Greek gods, theaters and Greek city councils, and Jews lived in some of them as a minority.

Crowds from the Decapolis follow Jesus (Matthew 4:25). Across the lake, in the land of the Gerasenes or Gadarenes (the manuscripts differ), Jesus frees a man from the legion of spirits, and the man becomes the first to announce Jesus in the Ten Cities (Mark 5:1–20; Matthew 8:28–34; Luke 8:26–39). Jesus later passes through the region and heals a deaf man (Mark 7:31–37). Many readers see these stories as a first step of the good news toward the Gentiles.
